title: The Bestiary
subtitle: Sea monsters, singing birds, and three demons who want to go home
blurb: Forget horns and pitchforks: tonight the book sends up a mermaid, a phoenix, a peacock, a star, and a wolf who is counting the years.

segments.t: Close your eyes and draw me a demon. Red skin, I expect. Horns. A tail with a point on it, and a pitchfork somewhere. It is a good drawing. It is also not in the book. I have been through all seventy-two entries, and not one of them is a red man with a tail.

Last night we kept company with lovers, liars and thieves. Tonight asks for nothing but your eyes. Because here is what the book really sends up the stairs. A sea monster. A mermaid. A phoenix that sings in a child's voice. A peacock. A star. A small boy on a dragon with two heads.

Welcome to the eighth night. I call it the Bestiary. A bestiary was a medieval book of beasts, real and imagined, each with its picture and its meaning. Twelve spirits tonight, and for once I care less about what they do than how they arrive. Three rooms. Water, fire, and a cabinet of wonders.

We begin under water. The thirtieth spirit is Forneus, a mighty and great marquis with twenty-nine legions. The book gives his shape in four words. A great sea monster. No scales counted, no teeth measured. Only something enormous, turning over in the dark. And what does the monster do? It teaches rhetoric, the art of speaking well. And then this.
He causeth men to have a Good Name, and to have the knowledge and understanding of Tongues. He maketh one to be beloved of his Foes as well as of his Friends.

A leviathan that gives lessons in charm. Swim up a little. The forty-second spirit is Vepar, a duke great and strong, with twenty-nine legions, and he appears like a mermaid. Yes, he. The book does not blink. Vepar governs the waters and guides ships laden with arms and armour. He has an ugly side, too. He can make a man die in three days of rotting wounds. But listen to his best trick.
And at the request of the Exorcist he can cause the seas to be right stormy and to appear full of ships.
To appear full of ships. Not to be. A phantom navy on the horizon, sails with nothing under them. Exorcist, by the way, is only the book's word for whoever is doing the calling.

Above the mermaid, the weather. Focalor, the forty-first spirit, a mighty duke and strong, with thirty legions. He comes as a man with a griffin's wings. A griffin is half eagle, half lion. Remember him.
His office is to slay Men, and to drown them in the Waters, and to overthrow Ships of War, for he hath Power over both Winds and Seas.

And yet the same entry says he will hurt no man or thing if he is told not to. A drowner with a safety catch. Then, almost in passing, the book adds that Focalor hopes to return to the Seventh Throne after a thousand years. Hold on to that sentence. I am coming back for it.

One more by the water, and the gentlest. Crocell, the forty-ninth, a duke great and strong, with forty-eight legions. He appears as an angel, speaking somewhat mystically of hidden things. He teaches geometry and the liberal sciences. He told Solomon he had belonged to the order of Powers before his fall. And he has two gifts.
He, at the Command of the Exorcist, will produce Great Noises like the Rushings of many Waters, although there be none. He warmeth Waters, and discovereth Baths.

The roar of a river in a dry room. Nothing wet, nothing moved, only the sound. A word on that order of Powers. Medieval theology sorted the angels into nine orders, like regiments, with names such as Thrones, Dominations and Powers. The book likes to note which regiment each spirit deserted.

threshold.q: Before we leave the shore. A sea monster who teaches charm, a mermaid with a ghost fleet, an angel who sounds like a river. If one of them could rise in front of you tonight, only to be looked at, which would you choose?

opts.label: The sea monster
opts.reply: Forneus. You want the big dark shape, and I do not blame you. Notice the book never describes him, and that is why he works. Four words, and you supplied the rest yourself. Every monster you have ever loved was mostly made by you. He would approve. He teaches rhetoric, after all.

opts.label: The ghost fleet
opts.reply: Vepar's ships. So you want to stand on the cliff and watch a hundred sails come out of the weather, knowing none of them is there. That is a taste for the uncanny. It is the right taste for this book, which is one long horizon full of things that only appear.

opts.label: Only the sound
opts.reply: Crocell, and from a safe distance. Sensible. A noise of water with no water is the one marvel tonight that needs nothing to exist. It is also, I notice, exactly what a frightened person hears in an empty room at night. The book may know more about ears than about angels.

segments.t: Then dry yourself off. The second room is warmer. The thirty-seventh spirit is Phenex, a great marquis with twenty legions. He appears like the phoenix, the bird that burns and rises from its own ashes. And he has the voice of a child.
He singeth many sweet notes before the Exorcist, which he must not regard, but by-and-by he must bid him put on Human Shape.

Which he must not regard. The song is so sweet that the book has to warn you off it. Once he takes human shape he speaks marvellously of all the sciences. And the book adds, flatly, that he is a poet, good and excellent. So Hell has a poet, and he reviews well.

Beside the bird, something with teeth. Haures, the sixty-fourth spirit, a great duke with thirty-six legions. First a leopard, mighty, terrible and strong. Then a man with flaming, fiery eyes and a most terrible face. He tells the truth about past, present and future, but only inside the triangle, that marked space from the third night. Outside it he lies. He burns up the enemies of whoever calls him. And if asked, he will talk about the creation of the world, and how he and the other spirits fell.

He is not the only one who talks about the fall. Marchosias, the thirty-fifth spirit, a great and mighty marquis with thirty legions. A wolf with a griffin's wings and a serpent's tail, vomiting fire. In the older printed lists the wolf is a she-wolf. He is a strong fighter, and he was once of the order of Dominations. And then the entry does something no personnel file should do.
He told his Chief, who was Solomon, that after 1,200 years he had hopes to return unto the Seventh Throne.

He had hopes. Stay with me, because this is the heart of the night. Three of tonight's spirits say it. Focalor the drowner, after a thousand years. Marchosias the wolf, after twelve hundred. Phenex the singing bird, after twelve hundred more. Nobody is certain what the Seventh Throne is, and the book never explains. The likeliest reading is a seat in the highest heaven, the place they held before they fell. Home, in other words.

Think what that does to the catalogue. In the middle of the ranks and the legions, three demons are counting the years. They are homesick. And the older writers would not let it stand. When Reginald Scot printed this list in English in fifteen eighty-four, the wolf's entry ended like this. I have modernised his spelling.
He was of the order of dominations, under him are thirty legions: he hopeth after twelve hundred years to return to the seventh throne, but he is deceived in that hope.
segments.src: Scot, Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), spelling modernised

segments.t: Deceived in that hope. Somebody felt the need to add it. The Lesser Key, copied a lifetime later, leaves the clause out. The hope simply stands, and no one corrects it. I do not know whether that was mercy or a tired copyist. I know which I prefer.

threshold.q: So I will ask you what the copyists could not agree on. A wolf, a drowner and a singing bird, all waiting out the centuries. Do the homesick demons deserve to go home?

opts.label: Let them go home
opts.reply: Soft heart. You are in old company. Origen, a Christian teacher of the third century, wondered whether in the end every fallen thing might be restored, and the church later condemned the idea. So you have just been gently heretical on behalf of a wolf. I think he would be touched.

opts.label: No. Scot was right
opts.reply: Strict, and orthodox. For most medieval theologians a fallen angel's choice was final, made once and with perfect clarity. No appeal, no parole. Which makes the hope stranger, not weaker. Somebody wrote it down knowing the official answer, and wrote it down anyway.

opts.label: It's a sales pitch
opts.reply: Sharp. A demon with a sad story is easier to trust, and a book that wants to be used has every reason to make its spirits sympathetic. I cannot rule that out. But notice that it worked on you well enough to need resisting. That is craft, whoever it belonged to.

segments.t: Whatever you decided, leave them to their counting. The third room is the one I promised you, the cabinet of wonders. Shelves, glass, labels. And in the first case, a star.

Decarabia, the sixty-ninth spirit, a great marquis with thirty legions. He appears as a star in a pentacle, a magical figure drawn as a charm. A point of light inside a diagram. Only when commanded does he put on the image of a man. And the star, of all things, is a naturalist.
His Office is to discover the Virtues of Birds and Precious Stones, and to make the Similitude of all kinds of Birds to fly before the Exorcist, singing and drinking as natural Birds do.

Where there are birds there is a peacock. Andrealphus, the sixty-fifth, a mighty marquis with thirty legions, arrives as a peacock with great noises. If you have ever heard a peacock, you know that is simple accuracy. He teaches geometry perfectly, and everything to do with measuring and astronomy. And he can transform a man into the likeness of a bird. Whether the man is asked first, the book does not say.

Next case. Oriax, the fifty-ninth, a great marquis with thirty legions. A lion with a serpent's tail, riding a mighty and strong horse, holding two great hissing serpents in his right hand. The old editor could not tell whether the tail belongs to the lion or the horse. Oriax teaches the virtues of the stars and the mansions of the planets, the houses astrologers gave each planet in the sky. He transforms men, and he hands out dignities.

And then the one that stops people. Volac, the sixty-second, a president mighty and great, with thirty-eight legions. He appears like a child with angel's wings, riding on a two-headed dragon. He gives true answers about hidden treasure, and he tells where serpents may be seen. A recent horror film borrowed his other name, Valak, and gave it to a ghostly nun. The book has no nun. The book has a little boy on a dragon, which I find worse.

Last in the cabinet, music. Amdusias, the sixty-seventh, a duke great and strong, with twenty-nine legions. He appears first as a unicorn. Then he stands in human shape, and things begin to be heard. Here is Scot again, in fifteen eighty-four.
He easily bringeth to pass, that trumpets and all musical instruments may be heard and not seen, and also that trees shall bend and incline, according to the conjuror's will.
segments.src: Scot, Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), spelling modernised

segments.t: Heard and not seen. An orchestra with nobody in it, and a forest bowing. By the time the Lesser Key is copied, that line has changed. The instruments are heard, it says, but not soon or immediately. It looks very like a copyist misreading not seen. I cannot prove it. But I enjoy a demon whose miracle became a delay. His seal is in your grimoire now, with eleven others.

Now, a confession about your eyes. Some of the pictures in your head are not yours. The Lesser Key has no illustrations of the spirits. Only the seals. The famous faces come from Paris, in eighteen sixty-three. You met that engraver's work on the sixth night, in Buer's wheel and the owl of Stolas. His name was Louis Le Breton, and he drew a whole set for a new edition of a demon dictionary by Collin de Plancy. The Dictionnaire Infernal.

If you have ever seen Volac on his dragon, or Amdusias among his trumpets, you have almost certainly seen Le Breton. Two hundred years after the manuscripts. So even the faces of the demons are a later invention. The book gave words. A Frenchman with a sharp pencil gave everyone the same dream.

So where did the words get their shapes? Go back to the griffin. Eagle and lion, joined at the waist. That is heraldry, the medieval art of the coat of arms, where a family is a lion, a leopard, a wolf, a unicorn. Now look at tonight's list again. Lion. Leopard. Wolf. Unicorn. Marquises and dukes, each with his own seal. These are coats of arms that walk.

That is my reading, not something the book states. But it fits how people drew what nobody had seen. You cannot picture the truly unknown. So you build it from parts you have. A wing from here, a tail from there, a child's voice in a burning bird. The seams are the point. The seams tell you it comes from somewhere else.

Tomorrow we follow that somewhere else all the way down. Because some of these names were prayed to long before they were feared. Storm gods. Queens of heaven. The ninth night is called Older Than Hell, and it is about how a god becomes a demon.

Until then. Close the cabinet. If you hear trumpets on the stairs, be patient. They are not soon, or immediately. And if something small sings to you very sweetly on the way up, you know the rule. Do not regard it.

glossary.def: A medieval book of beasts, real and imaginary, each described with a picture and a moral. The Goetia's spirits borrow much of their look from the same tradition.
The nine ranks into which medieval theology sorted the angels, including Thrones, Dominations and Powers. The Goetia often says which order a spirit belonged to before it fell.
The place three spirits of the Goetia say they hope to return to after a thousand or twelve hundred years. The book never explains it; it is usually read as their lost seat in heaven.

A French dictionary of demons by Collin de Plancy. Its illustrated edition of eighteen sixty-three, with engravings after Louis Le Breton, gave many Goetic spirits the faces people know today, including the wheel-legged Buer and the owl Stolas. Those pictures are not in the Lesser Key.
The medieval system of coats of arms, in which families and offices were shown as lions, leopards, griffins and other beasts, often stitched together from several animals.
